books.title: The radio course book
books.handedLine: The club secretary hands you the radio course book.

pages.title: Channel 16 and channel 70
pages.text:
Channel 16 is the calling and distress channel. It is for four things only: distress, urgency, safety and calling. A call on 16 is how you reach another station for the first time; it is never the place to chat.

Channel 70 is different. It carries digital selective calling, the DSC alerts that radios send to each other as data. You never speak on channel 70: it is for digital alerts only, not for voice.

pages.title: Calling, and the working channels
pages.text:
To call a station, say its name up to three times, then "this is", then your own boat's name: "Skjærvik harbour, Skjærvik harbour, Skjærvik harbour, this is sailing yacht Marit, Marit, Marit, over."

When the station answers, do not carry on talking on 16. Agree a working channel and both of you switch to it. That keeps 16 free for the next distress call or the next stranger trying to reach someone. Ship-to-ship working channels are set aside for talk between boats; the harbour office names its own working channel when it answers.

A radio check, to find out whether your set works, is made on a working channel and never on 16: call a friendly station and ask for a radio check. If it answers "loud and clear", it is receiving you strongly and you can be understood. If it says weak or unreadable, check the aerial, the plug and the power setting, and ask again.

pages.title: Over, out and the alphabet
pages.text:
Say "over" when you have finished speaking and expect a reply. Say "out" when the conversation is finished and no reply is wanted. They mean opposite things, so do not say "over and out".

When a name or a call sign must be understood over a poor signal, spell it with the phonetic alphabet: Alfa, Bravo, Charlie, Delta, Echo, Foxtrot, Golf, Hotel, India, Juliett, Kilo, Lima, Mike, November, Oscar, Papa, Quebec, Romeo, Sierra, Tango, Uniform, Victor, Whiskey, X-ray, Yankee, Zulu. Kvitnes is Kilo Victor India Tango November Echo Sierra.

pages.title: The licence
pages.text:
A VHF radio may be used only by someone who holds the operator's certificate: here, the radio ticket, which this course earns. The boat needs a call sign as well, from her ship radio licence (which is not one of your tickets); it gives her the call sign and an MMSI, the nine-digit number her radio sends in a DSC alert.

Without the ticket you may not make a call, and the coast radio reports a call made without one.

pages.title: Mayday, Pan-Pan and Sécurité
pages.text:
Three words say how serious a call is. Each is said three times, and a call that begins with one of them begins on channel 16.

MAYDAY is distress: grave and imminent danger to a person or to the boat, and immediate help needed. A fire, a boat sinking, a person lost overboard whom you cannot recover. Use the word for nothing else, not even in conversation.

PAN-PAN is urgency: a message about the safety of a person or of the boat, but no immediate danger. An engine failed and the boat drifting toward rocks, but with time still in hand.

SÉCURITÉ is safety: a message about the safety of navigation, such as a warning of a hazard, or a weather warning.

pages.title: The Mayday message
pages.text:
With no DSC, send the call by voice on channel 16, in this order:
1. MAYDAY, MAYDAY, MAYDAY.
2. This is sailing yacht Marit, Marit, Marit: your boat's name three times.
3. Your call sign and MMSI.
4. MAYDAY, Marit: once more.
5. Your position: latitude and longitude, or a bearing and distance from a mark, or "position unknown".
6. The nature of your distress: sinking, fire, collision.
7. The help you need: "I require immediate assistance."
8. The number of people on board.
9. Anything else that helps: the boat's length and colour, a liferaft.
10. "Over."

Speak slowly and clearly. The order is easy to lose under stress, so learn it: Mayday, identity, position, distress, assistance, number on board, other information, over.

pages.title: The DSC alert, and keeping silent
pages.text:
A DSC radio has a red distress button under a cover. Lift the cover, press it and hold it until the radio confirms it has sent the alert. The alert goes out on channel 70 as data: your boat's identity (the MMSI), your position if the radio is wired to a position receiver, the time and, if you chose one, the nature of the distress. It repeats until another station acknowledges it.

The radio then switches to channel 16. Wait a few seconds, then send the voice Mayday call and message as on the page before: the alert does not replace the voice call.

When you hear a Mayday that is not yours, stay silent. Distress traffic has priority over everything else: listen on the channel and do not call the boat or carry on with your own talk.

books.title: The coastal skipper course book
books.handedLine: The club secretary hands you the coastal skipper course book.

pages.title: Lights at night
pages.text:
Red to port, green to starboard, white astern. A boat shows a red light on her port (left) side and a green light on her starboard (right) side. Each sidelight shines over 112.5 degrees, from straight ahead to 22.5 degrees abaft the beam. A white sternlight shines over the remaining 135 degrees astern. A power-driven boat adds a white masthead light shining forward over 225 degrees, the same arc as the two sidelights together.

So a red light on its own means you are looking at the other boat's port side; green, her starboard side; white, her stern.

pages.title: Under sail and under power
pages.text:
A sailing boat under sail shows the sidelights and the sternlight and no white masthead light. (On a boat under 20 metres the three may be combined in one lantern at the top of the mast.)

When she runs her engine she is a power-driven boat in the rules, even with the sails up: at night she shows the masthead light as well, and by day she hangs a black cone, point down, forward where it can best be seen (a boat under 12 metres need not). Motor-sailing counts as motoring.

pages.title: Who gives way
pages.text:
Two sailing boats, wind on opposite sides: the boat with the wind on her port side (on port tack) keeps clear. If you are on port tack and cannot tell which side the other has her wind, keep clear.

Two sailing boats on the same tack: the windward boat, the one nearer the wind, keeps clear of the leeward boat.

Overtaking: any boat that overtakes keeps clear of the boat she overtakes, sail or power. A boat is overtaking if she comes up from more than 22.5 degrees abaft the other's beam, where she would see only the other's sternlight.

Power and sail: a power-driven boat keeps clear of a sailing boat. The exceptions are boats that can only navigate inside a narrow channel: a sailing boat must not get in their way. The ferry that runs the channel to Hestholmen is one. A boat fishing, or not under command, also has the right of way over a boat under sail.

Two power-driven boats meeting head-on both alter course to starboard and pass port to port. Two power-driven boats crossing: the one that has the other on her starboard side keeps clear, and must not cross ahead of her.

pages.title: Seeing the danger
pages.text:
Keep a lookout all the time, by eye and by ear. To tell whether an approaching boat is a danger, take a compass bearing on her and take it again: if the bearing does not change appreciably while she comes nearer, there is a risk of collision, and you should assume it.

When you act, act early, and make the change large and bold, so that the other boat can see at once what you have done. A string of small alterations is not seen.

In sight of another boat a power-driven boat may sound her intentions: one short blast means "I am altering my course to starboard"; two short blasts, "I am altering my course to port"; three short blasts, "my engine is going astern". At least five short and rapid blasts mean you doubt what the other boat is doing.

pages.title: Fog signals
pages.text:
In fog, slow down and sound your signal at intervals of not more than two minutes. A prolonged blast is a long one, four to six seconds.

A power-driven boat making way through the water: one prolonged blast.

A power-driven boat underway but stopped, making no way: two prolonged blasts in succession, about two seconds apart.

A sailing boat (and a boat fishing, or towing): one prolonged blast followed by two short blasts, the same every two minutes. Whatever you are, keep a lookout and listen.

pages.title: The weather
pages.text:
The Beaufort scale gives the wind a force. Force 4, moderate breeze: 11 to 16 knots. Force 5, fresh breeze: 17 to 21 knots. Force 6, strong breeze: 22 to 27 knots. Force 7, near gale: 28 to 33 knots. Force 8, gale: 34 to 40 knots. On a 28-footer force 6 is a day to reef early or stay in, with the sea turning short and steep; force 7 is a day for harbour.

Fog at sea forms when warm, damp air passes over a colder sea and is cooled to its dew point. The weather line gives both numbers. When the dew point is at or above the sea temperature, fog is likely if the wind is light. When the sea is many degrees warmer than the dew point, as with a dew point of 6 and a sea of 13, the air is not cooled to its dew point and there will be no fog.

A lee shore is a shore that the wind blows onto. If the engine fails or the boat will not claw off, the wind sets her onto it. Keep sea room, and plan so that you can get away from it, to windward or into shelter.

pages.title: The passage plan
pages.text:
Before you cast off, plan the passage, and write it down. The distance and the time. The forecast for the whole window, not only for the start: the weather line, and the days after. Daylight: when it gets dark, and whether you will arrive after dark. Fuel: the rule of thirds, a third to get there, a third to get back and a third in reserve, worked from the litres an hour the engine burns; the trip plan tells you the litres needed and the litres aboard. The tide, where it matters.

A bolt hole: a harbour or an anchorage you can reach if the plan goes wrong. The trip plan names the shelter on the way. And tell someone ashore where you are going and when you expect to be back.

pages.title: The engine
pages.text:
A voltage drop is what a meter reads across one connection while current flows through it: a terminal clamp, a cable end. With the starter cranking, a good connection reads almost nothing. A reading of a volt or more across a single clamp means resistance there, corrosion or a loose clamp, and the voltage is being lost as heat in it. Clean it and tighten it.

Watch the exhaust water. At every start, look for water at the outlet. A weak flow comes first: the raw-water impeller or the intake is failing. The overheat alarm comes later, when the damage has begun, so a weak flow is the time to stop and look, not the alarm.

Water in the fuel is heavier than diesel and settles in the bowl of the primary filter. Drain the bowl and look. In a seaway the tank is stirred up and the water reaches the filter: the engine fires and dies just when you need it. A bowl with water in it means water in the tank, so drain it again on other days and then fit a new element. Keeping the tank full leaves no room for damp air to condense.

questions.text: What is channel 16 for?
options: Chat between friendly boats
Distress, urgency, safety and calling
Weather forecasts and tide times only
Booking a berth with the harbour
questions.source: ITU Radio Regulations Appendix 18 (VHF maritime channels); https://www.sea.net/education/vhf-radio-guide
questions.checked: sea.net guide: 16 is for distress, safety and initial contact, 'not the channel for conversation'. Appendix 18 itself not read.

questions.text: You have called a boat on channel 16 and it has answered. What do you do next?
options: Carry on talking on channel 16
Switch to channel 70 and talk there
Say 'out' and call again on 16
Agree a working channel and both switch to it
questions.checked: sea.net guide: 'Initiate on 16; move to a working channel; complete the conversation; close the contact.'

questions.text: What is channel 70 used for?
options: Calling ferries and the harbour
Voice calls to the coast radio
Digital selective calling alerts, never voice
Weather forecasts
questions.checked: sea.net table: 70 is 'DSC digital distress (do not voice transmit)'.

questions.text: When may you say MAYDAY?
options: When a person or the boat is in grave and imminent danger and needs immediate help
Whenever you want to be heard quickly
When the engine fails in a calm harbour
At the start of every call on 16
questions.checked: portreath-harbour.org: 'Grave and Imminent Danger to a Person, Ship ... Requiring Immediate Assistance'; the word is only for distress. Article number from memory, not read.

questions.text: What is a PAN-PAN call for?
options: Grave and imminent danger needing immediate help
An urgent message about the safety of a person or the boat, but not an immediate danger
A warning of a navigational hazard
A radio check
questions.checked: portreath-harbour.org and sea.net: urgency, 'urgent but not immediately life-threatening'.

questions.text: What does a call beginning SÉCURITÉ introduce?
options: A distress message from another boat
A request for a radio check
A message about the safety of navigation, such as a hazard or a weather warning
A message from the harbourmaster about your berth
questions.checked: portreath-harbour.org: 'Transmissions concerning the safety of navigation are prefixed with SECURITE.'

questions.text: How does a voice Mayday call begin?
options: MAYDAY three times, then the boat's name three times
MAYDAY once, then your position
The boat's name once, then MAYDAY once
PAN-PAN three times, then MAYDAY once
questions.checked: portreath-harbour.org: 'Mayday three times, then your vessel's name three times'; sea.net agrees. Article number from memory.

questions.text: In a Mayday message, what comes straight after your boat's name, call sign and MMSI?
options: The nature of your distress
The number of people on board
The word 'over'
Your position
questions.source: UK GMDSS distress procedure (RYA SRC syllabus); https://portreath-harbour.org/distress-proceedures
questions.checked: portreath-harbour.org order: names, call sign and MMSI, 'Mayday' once with the name once, then position, nature of distress, assistance, people on board, other information, 'Over'.

questions.text: After the nature of the distress, which two things does a Mayday message give?
options: The harbour you left, and the time
The help you need, and the number of people on board
A radio check, and the weather
Your fuel, and your insurer
questions.source: UK GMDSS distress procedure (RYA SRC syllabus); https://portreath-harbour.org/distress-proceedures
questions.checked: portreath-harbour.org list: nature of distress, 'I require immediate assistance', total number of people on board, other useful information.

questions.text: What does a DSC distress alert carry?
options: Only the word Mayday
A voice message of fifteen seconds
Your boat's identity (MMSI), position and time, and the nature of the distress if you chose one
The names of your crew
questions.source: ITU Radio Regulations Appendix 18 / RYA SRC syllabus; https://portreath-harbour.org/distress-proceedures
questions.checked: portreath-harbour.org: data burst on 70 'with your MMSI, position, time, and nature of distress (if selected)'.

questions.text: You have sent a DSC distress alert. What do you do next?
options: Send the voice Mayday call and message on channel 16
Nothing, the alert is enough
Send a PAN-PAN on channel 70
Switch the radio off to save the battery
questions.source: UK GMDSS distress procedure (RYA SRC syllabus); https://portreath-harbour.org/distress-proceedures
questions.checked: portreath-harbour.org: after the alert the screen switches to 16; wait 15 seconds, then give the voice call and message. soundingsonline.com agrees: the alert does not replace the voice call.

questions.text: How do you open a routine call to the harbour?
options: Your own boat's name, then the harbour's name, then 'over and out'
MAYDAY, then the harbour's name
Your name only, once, and then silence
The harbour's name, then 'this is' and your own boat's name
questions.checked: sea.net guide: say the called vessel's name three times, then 'this is' and your own name. Article number from memory.

questions.text: Where do you make a radio check?
options: On channel 16, so that everyone hears it
On channel 70, so that it is digital
On a working channel, not on channel 16
At the start of every call
questions.source: RYA SRC syllabus; UK Coastguard guidance; https://www.sailboat-cruising.com/correct-VHF-radio-procedure.html
questions.checked: Several boating sites agree (search 2026-11): not on 16, on an open working channel. Not read at the regulator's own page.

questions.text: Another boat answers your radio check: 'loud and clear'. What does that tell you?
options: It receives you strongly and can understand you
Your papers are in order
You must move to channel 70
You must repeat the check on 16
questions.checked: Informal sources only (boating sites, forums): replies like 'loud and clear', 'weak but readable'. UNVERIFIED against the syllabus.

questions.text: What does 'over' mean on the radio?
options: The conversation is finished
I have finished speaking and expect a reply
This is an emergency
Switch to channel 16
questions.source: ITU Radio Regulations Appendix 14 / ICAO radiotelephony procedure; https://www.sea.net/education/vhf-radio-guide
questions.checked: sea.net: 'over' ends a transmission that expects a reply.

questions.text: What does 'out' mean on the radio?
options: I have finished speaking and expect a reply
Say that again
I am switching to a working channel
The conversation is finished and no reply is wanted
questions.checked: sea.net: 'out' ends the conversation; a boating site notes 'over and out' is contradictory.

questions.text: What do you need to use a VHF radio on your boat?
options: Nothing, if you stay in harbour
Only the licence to handle the boat
The radio ticket, and a call sign for the boat
The coastal skipper ticket
questions.source: Ofcom, Ships' radio licence and operator's certificate; https://www.ofcom.org.uk/manage-your-licence/radiocommunication-licences/ships-radio
questions.checked: Ofcom/ybw.com: ship licence with call sign and MMSI, operator holds the SRC. UK rule; the game's rule is Amit's (design note 012).

questions.text: Why do you spell a boat's name or call sign with the phonetic alphabet?
options: So that nobody else can understand it
So that the letters are not misheard over a poor signal
Because every word on the radio must be spelled
Because it is quicker
questions.source: ITU Radio Regulations Appendix 14 (spelling alphabet); https://www.qsl.net/sccarc/file/itu.htm
questions.checked: The spelling alphabet's use stated in several sources; the word list matches the ICAO list.

questions.text: In the phonetic alphabet, which word stands for the letter K?
options: Kilo
Karl
King
Kappa
questions.source: ITU Radio Regulations Appendix 14 / ICAO spelling alphabet; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NATO_phonetic_alphabet
questions.checked: Word list checked in search results (Alfa ... Kilo ... Zulu).

questions.text: You hear a Mayday from a boat that is not yours. What do you do?
options: Call the boat for details
Carry on with your own call on 16
Send a PAN-PAN
Stay silent and listen on the channel
questions.checked: portreath-harbour.org: all stations hearing a Mayday must cease transmitting and keep listening; distress calls take priority.

questions.text: At night you can see only a red light on another boat. Which side of her are you looking at?
options: Her starboard side
Her stern
Her port side
Her bow
questions.checked: Arcs and colours confirmed in search results: green starboard, red port, white astern.

questions.text: Over what arc does the white sternlight shine?
options: 135 degrees
112.5 degrees
225 degrees
360 degrees
questions.checked: Search results (ialacolreg.com, flashcards): sternlight covers the remaining 135 degrees; sidelights 112.5 each; masthead 225.

questions.text: A boat shows a white light over 225 degrees ahead, as well as her sidelights and sternlight. What is she?
options: A sailing boat under sail
A boat at anchor
A power-driven boat
A boat fishing
questions.checked: The masthead light shares the 225 degree forward arc; a sailing vessel shows no masthead light (Rule 25), per search results.

questions.text: A sailing boat under sail at night shows:
options: A white masthead light and a sternlight only
Sidelights and a sternlight, and no white masthead light
A white masthead light and sidelights
A single all-round white light
questions.checked: cultofsea.com / ialacolreg.com: 'A sailing vessel underway shall exhibit sidelights and a sternlight.'

questions.text: By day a sailing boat has her sails up and her engine running. What does she hang forward?
options: A black cone, point down
A black cone, point up
A black ball
Nothing: she is sailing
questions.checked: Search results: a sailing vessel also propelled by machinery shows forward a conical shape, apex downwards; under 12 m not required.

questions.text: Two sailing boats meet, one with the wind on her port side and one on her starboard. Which keeps clear?
options: The one with the wind on her starboard side
The one with the wind on her port side
The faster one
The one nearer the shore
questions.checked: Wikipedia COLREGs summary: the vessel with the wind on its port side keeps out of the way.

questions.text: Two sailing boats are on the same tack. Which keeps clear?
options: The leeward boat
The smaller boat
The one that is overtaking
The windward boat
questions.checked: Wikipedia COLREGs summary: when both have the wind on the same side, the windward vessel keeps out of the way.

questions.text: A motor boat comes up astern of your sailing boat and means to pass. Who keeps clear?
options: You, because she is power-driven
Neither: both alter to starboard
The motor boat, because she is overtaking
You, because she is faster
questions.checked: Wikipedia: the overtaking vessel keeps clear; for sailing vessels Rule 13 takes precedence over Rules 12 and 18.

questions.text: You are under sail in the narrow channel to Hestholmen and the ferry, which can only navigate inside it, comes up. Who must not get in the other's way?
options: You must not impede the ferry
The ferry, because you are under sail
Neither: both alter to starboard
The ferry, because you are smaller
questions.checked: Wikipedia: a sailing vessel must not impede a vessel that can navigate only within a narrow channel; Rule 18(a) keeps Rule 9 above the sail-over-power rule.

questions.text: A motor boat and a sailing boat meet in open water. Which keeps clear?
options: The sailing boat
The motor boat
The one on the left
The slower one
questions.checked: Rule 18(a) text fetched: a power-driven vessel underway shall keep out of the way of a sailing vessel (except where Rules 9, 10 and 13 require otherwise).

questions.text: Two power-driven boats meet head-on. What does each do?
options: Alters course to port
The slower keeps clear
Alters course to starboard and passes port to port
Holds her course and sounds five short blasts
questions.checked: Wikipedia: both alter course to starboard so as to pass port to port.

questions.text: You take a compass bearing of an approaching boat, and a minute later it has not changed. What does that tell you?
options: She will pass clear astern
She is slowing down
Nothing: a bearing means nothing without radar
There is a risk of collision
questions.checked: Rule 7(d)(i) text fetched: risk shall be deemed to exist if the compass bearing of an approaching vessel does not appreciably change.

questions.text: You decide to alter course to avoid a collision. How?
options: Early, with a large and bold alteration the other boat can see
Late, to be sure she has not changed course
With a string of small alterations
By sounding five short blasts and holding on
questions.checked: Wikipedia summary of Rule 8: 'a large and bold angle of course alteration'. Rule text not read in full.

questions.text: A power-driven boat in sight sounds one short blast. What does it mean?
options: I am altering my course to port
I am altering my course to starboard
My engine is going astern
I doubt what you are doing
questions.checked: Fetched: one short = starboard, two short = port, three short = astern; five short and rapid = doubt (34(d)).

questions.text: In fog your engine is running and you are making way. What do you sound, at least every two minutes?
options: One prolonged blast
Two prolonged blasts
One prolonged and two short blasts
Five short blasts
questions.checked: Rule 35(a) text fetched: one prolonged blast at intervals of not more than 2 minutes.

questions.text: In fog you are under sail. What do you sound, at least every two minutes?
options: One prolonged blast
Two prolonged blasts
Three short blasts
One prolonged blast followed by two short blasts
questions.checked: Rule 35(c) text fetched: sailing vessel (with NUC, RAM, fishing ...) sounds one prolonged followed by two short.

questions.text: What wind speed is force 6 on the Beaufort scale?
options: 11 to 16 knots
17 to 21 knots
22 to 27 knots
34 to 40 knots
questions.checked: Met Office table via search: force 6 strong breeze 22-27 kt.

questions.text: What is the top of force 4 on the Beaufort scale?
options: 16 knots
11 knots
21 knots
27 knots
questions.checked: Met Office table via search: force 4 moderate breeze 11-16 kt.

questions.text: The weather line says: dew point 6, sea 13. What does it tell you about fog?
options: Fog is likely: the sea is warm
None is likely: the sea is far warmer than the dew point
Fog is certain in the morning
Nothing, fog depends only on the wind
questions.source: Met Office / Bureau of Meteorology notes on sea fog; https://www.bom.gov.au/aviation/data/education/hwp-fog.pdf
questions.checked: Search: sea fog forms when warm, moist air is cooled to its dew point over a colder sea; if the dew point is below the sea temperature fog is unlikely. The game's own fog margin is in weather.json.

questions.text: What is a lee shore?
options: A shore that the wind blows onto
A shore with no wind
A shore that is always sheltered
A shore with a lighthouse
questions.source: RYA Day Skipper / Coastal Skipper theory; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lee_shore
questions.checked: Sources agree: the shore on the lee side of a vessel, the wind blowing toward it; keep sea room.

questions.text: For a passage you work out the fuel by the rule of thirds. What is it?
options: A third now, a third at the half way, a third in the tank at the end
Enough for a third of the passage under power
A third to go, a third to come back, a third in reserve
A third of the tank for the engine, the rest for the stove
questions.checked: boattests101.com via search: outbound third, return third, emergency reserve third. A rule of thumb, not a regulation.

questions.text: What is a bolt hole in a passage plan?
options: The hole the exhaust runs through
A harbour or anchorage you can reach if the passage goes wrong
The last harbour on the passage
A place to leave the boat for the winter
questions.checked: Search result: shelter along the route, contingency harbours. Term also in common use among sailors; Amit to confirm the word.

questions.text: With the starter cranking, a meter across one terminal clamp reads more than a volt. What does it mean?
options: The battery is fully charged
The starter motor is worn out
The alternator belt is slipping
There is resistance in that connection, probably corrosion or a loose clamp
questions.checked: Voltage drop across a connection under load indicates resistance there (Ohm's law); limits vary by source (0.1 to 0.5 V per circuit) so the book and the question avoid a threshold apart from 'a volt or more'. UNVERIFIED against ABYC E-11 itself.

questions.text: At the start you see only a weak trickle of water at the exhaust outlet. What does it mean?
options: The raw-water impeller or intake is failing: stop and look
The engine is running well
The overheat alarm will sound at once
The fuel is dirty
questions.checked: nauticed.org: check raw-water outflow at the exhaust at every start; weak flow means the cooling is failing. 'Weak flow comes before the alarm' is common practice, not a quoted rule.

questions.text: The bowl of your primary fuel filter has a line of water at the bottom. What do you do?
options: Leave it: water burns off
Drain it, and drain it again on other days before fitting a new element
Fit a new element at once and say no more
Top up the tank with fresh diesel on top
questions.checked: yacht.de: water settles in the bowl; motion stirs the tank; drain regularly. 'Three separate days' is the game's own fix (sloop28.json), not a standard.
